title: Ancient Footprints Reveal a Vanishing Lake at White Sands
summary:
Long ago, people walked beside a great lake in what is now White Sands National Park in New Mexico. Their footprints, left between 23,500 and 21,700 years ago, survived in the sand. Now scientists have studied the ground around those prints to rebuild the lost world those walkers knew.

The same team that pioneered dating the footprints in 2021 went further in a new study in Science Advances. It examined 20 layers containing human footprints in place, tracks of large ancient animals, and straight marks left by historic wheels. Radiocarbon dating of conifer pollen, combined with ages of aquatic seeds, refined the timeline.

The evidence points to what the team called a complete overturning of the environment, from a perennial lake to a playa, or dry lake bed, during the height of the ice age. At the start of the timeline, Lake Otero filled much of the basin, the surrounding mountains held conifer forests, and temperatures were about 4 degrees Celsius colder than today. Then temperatures began to rise. The lake shrank, forests declined, and oak and sagebrush crept in as evaporation increased.

Sharper climate swings sat on top of that slow change. A dry period coincides with a rapid climatic change recorded thousands of miles away in Greenland ice cores, the researchers report. The earliest footprints appear around that transition, and footprints continue at intervals as the lake retreated. Bennett and Reynolds wrote in The Conversation that people visited repeatedly amid substantial environmental change.

Computer modeling helped explain the pattern. In the team's virtual world, people moved around a fluctuating lake and left footprints when they crossed mud. Prints disappeared unless changing water levels buried and preserved them, so footprint surfaces occur as irregular pulses clustering around periods of climatic and hydrological change, just as the model predicted.
why_it_matters: Footprints show how people kept returning even as their world changed, which helps us understand how people may cope when climates and landscapes shift.

A playa is a dry lake bed.

background_read: Footprints can survive when wet ground is buried and protected, so they can tell scientists where people and animals walked long ago.
At White Sands, scientists studied the ground around ancient footprints to rebuild a world that has changed greatly, from a large lake to a dry lake bed.
As the climate warmed, the lake shrank, forests gave way to drier plants, and sharper dry spells came and went on top of that slow change.
Computer models helped the team test how moving water and changing lake levels could leave footprints only at certain times.
